executive_summary.title: Executive Summary
executive_summary.content: Traditional vector cosine similarity approaches for retrieval-augmented generation fall short when detecting subtle negations and numerical errors [cite_cite_1]. By breaking down generated text into atomic factual claims and applying calibrated Natural Language Inference (NLI) models, systems achieve significantly higher citation precision [cite_cite_2]. Furthermore, implementing selective two-stage verification strategies can dramatically reduce computational overhead without sacrificing recall on critical hallucinations [cite_cite_3].

claims.text: Vector cosine similarity between generated text and source chunks fails to identify subtle negation and numerical hallucinations, with false-positive attribution rates reaching 34%.
Decomposing answers into atomic factual claims and evaluating them using calibrated Natural Language Inference (NLI) models increases citation precision from 62% to 91% on open-domain QA benchmarks.

claims.text: Applying selective two-stage verification reduces verification cost by 55% while maintaining a 94% recall on critical hallucinations.

sections.title: NLI Verification and Performance Metrics
sections.content: Evaluating generation accuracy via vector cosine similarity leaves an opening for high false-positive attribution rates, which can reach up to 34% when handling subtle negations and numerical inaccuracies [cite_cite_4]. Utilizing Natural Language Inference to check atomic claims substantially enhances precision from 62% up to 91% [cite_cite_5]. However, cross-encoder verification introduces performance overhead, adding an average latency of 180ms per query on 8-core CPU instances for up to 10 atomic claims [cite_cite_6]. This latency can be mitigated through selective two-stage filtering [cite_cite_9].

executive_summary.title: Executive Summary
executive_summary.content: Traditional vector cosine similarity approaches for retrieval-augmented generation fall short when detecting subtle negations and numerical errors [cite_cite_1]. By breaking down generated text into atomic factual claims and applying calibrated Natural Language Inference (NLI) models, systems achieve significantly higher citation precision [cite_cite_2]. Furthermore, implementing selective two-stage verification strategies can dramatically reduce computational overhead without sacrificing recall on critical hallucinations [cite_cite_3].

sections.title: NLI Verification and Performance Metrics
sections.content: Evaluating generation accuracy via vector cosine similarity leaves an opening for high false-positive attribution rates, which can reach up to 34% when handling subtle negations and numerical inaccuracies [cite_cite_4]. Utilizing Natural Language Inference to check atomic claims substantially enhances precision from 62% up to 91% [cite_cite_5]. However, cross-encoder verification introduces performance overhead, adding an average latency of 180ms per query on 8-core CPU instances for up to 10 atomic claims [cite_cite_6]. This latency can be mitigated through selective two-stage filtering [cite_cite_9].
